701.title: The prince's unease
701.hook: the road cleared of the old and sick, yet the gods place an old man in his path (Buddhacarita 3)
701.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers return to the sights of old age, sickness and death when teaching impermanence, and the scenes are painted on temple walls and told to children in Buddhist communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday: life in the palace, every comfort arranged by a king afraid his son will leave. Your line: a father's fear.

Orders go out across the city. Sweep the royal road. Hang garlands. Set out banners and flowers. And one more order, the strange one: anyone old, anyone sick, anyone suffering, keep them off the road today. The prince has asked to see the gardens outside the walls, and the king, Shuddhodana, has said yes, on one condition. The world his son sees will have the hard parts taken out. By the time the chariot rolls through the gate, the street is perfect. Faces at every window. Not a single bent back in sight.

segments.voice: First, the crowd. People hurry to rooftops and windows to catch sight of the prince going by, and they look at him with delight. It's a parade, and for a moment the king's plan seems to work. Second, the gap. The road has been cleared; nobody old should be there. So the poem says the gods of the pure abodes made one: an old man appears in the prince's path, bent over, white-haired, leaning on a stick. The wall the king built was solid. Something came through it anyway. Third, the question. The prince turns to his charioteer and asks what this is. The charioteer answers simply: this is old age. It takes beauty and strength and memory. This man was a child once, and grew, and this is where the years have brought him. Then the question that matters. Will this happen to me? The answer is yes. To you, and to everyone. Fourth, the unease. The prince is shaken to the core. He can't enjoy the gardens, and asks to turn back. The king's whole plan was about keeping things out. The poem's answer is that some truths don't need permission.

702.title: The sick and the dead
702.hook: the prince asks the charioteer, and the world goes gray (Buddhacarita 3)
702.howItsDone: Some Buddhists, especially in monastic settings, reflect regularly on sickness, aging and death as part of practice, and Buddhist funerals can include chanting on impermanence.

segments.voice: Yesterday: old age, the first sight to slip past the king's cleared road. Your line: it gets through anyway.

Who is that man? A question a child might ask from the back seat of a car. The prince keeps asking it in this canto, and each answer takes something away. First, a man by the road with a swollen belly, breathing hard, leaning on others, crying out. Then a group of men carrying something on a frame, wrapped in cloth, with people walking behind them weeping. The palace wall has already cracked once. Now the poem widens the crack, one honest answer at a time.
screen: `WHO IS THAT MAN?` → `A SICK MAN BY THE ROAD.` → `A BODY CARRIED, PEOPLE WEEPING.`

segments.voice: First, sickness. The charioteer explains: this man is ill. Something in his body has gone wrong, and it has brought him low. Can it happen to anyone? Yes. The prince is shaken again, wondering how the crowds can be cheerful with this so close. Second, death. The poem says the gods moved the charioteer to tell the truth, even though the king would rather he didn't. This man has died, he says. He is like a log now; his family carried him out, and they are weeping. Is this the end for everyone? It is. High or low, it comes to all. Third, the gray. The same crowds, the same banners, the same gardens. Nothing outside has moved, but for him the color has drained out of it. He wonders aloud how people can go about laughing and careless when death is certain and close. That astonishment has an echo in the Dhammapada. In Max Müller's translation: "How is there laughter, how is there joy, as this world is always burning?" And fourth, where it leaves him. Not sunk. He keeps asking, and the question has turned outward: how can a whole street laugh beside this? That puzzle about other people, more than his own sadness, is what the next cantos follow. The garden, a friend's advice, and the night ride out of the city all grow from it.

Not fixing, just holding; when the mind runs off, come back to the breath.

703.title: The women in the garden
703.hook: the women are sent to charm him, and he stays unmoved (Buddhacarita 4)
703.howItsDone: Some Buddhist teachers use the garden scene when speaking about sense pleasures and restraint, and in temple murals the prince is sometimes shown seated calmly among dancers and musicians.

segments.voice: Yesterday: death, the charioteer's last answer, and the world gone gray. Your line: the world goes gray.

The king has heard. His son came home from the road shaken, and now he won't stop thinking about old age and death. So the king reaches for the tool he trusts. He sends the prince to a beautiful garden outside the city, and sends the women of the court with him. Their task is plain: delight him, bring him back to the life of pleasure, make him forget what he saw. Music under the trees. Flowers. Laughter by the water. The poem lingers in this garden, and every line is built to pull a young man's attention away from one thought.
screen: `THE KING TRIES AGAIN.` → `A GARDEN, MUSIC, THE COURT'S WOMEN.` → `MAKE HIM FORGET.`

segments.voice: First, the women. They didn't choose this. They were sent, by a king, with a task. At first, the poem says, they hold back, shy before the prince. Then they're urged on, and they do what they were told: they sing and dance, tease and whisper, wander close in the flowering garden, described with all the color and play of court poetry. Second, the prince. He doesn't scold them or run. He simply isn't moved. He looks at the young women, bright and laughing, and sees what the road just taught him: this beauty will age, these bodies will sicken, these lives will end. He's not cold toward them. He's thinking about them more truly than the garden wants him to. Third, steadiness. Unmoved doesn't mean frozen, or proud, or disgusted. In the Anguttara Nikaya the Buddha names eight worldly conditions, gain and loss, good name and bad name, praise and blame, pleasure and pain, and describes a mind they don't overturn. In the garden only the pleasant half is pulling, and steadiness looks like quiet. And fourth, the cost to the king. Another remedy has failed, and the poem blames no one in the garden. The women did what they were asked. The prince did what he couldn't help. And before he goes home, a friend will try.

704.title: Udayin's advice
704.hook: a friend urges him to enjoy life while he's young; the prince answers about aging (Buddhacarita 4)
704.howItsDone: Some Buddhist teachers describe sense pleasures as impermanent rather than evil in themselves, and this conversation can be retold as an example of disagreeing with kindness.

segments.voice: Yesterday: steadiness, the prince unmoved among the women in the garden. Your line: unmoved.

Look, I'm saying this because I care. You're too serious. Relax. You've got your whole life for the heavy stuff. In the garden, the friend who takes the prince aside is Udayin, the son of the king's priest, a young man the prince knows well. He has watched the women try and fail, so he makes the case for pleasure himself. It's a good case. The poem lets him make it fully, and that's what makes the prince's answer worth hearing.

segments.voice: First, the argument. Udayin speaks frankly, as a friend. Even if your heart isn't in it, he says, be courteous to these women; turning away from them is unkind. Then he reaches for old stories: great sages of the past were won over by love and pleasure, so why should you hold out? And his last point is the one friends still make: enjoy these things now, while you're young. There's time later for the forest. Second, how the prince listens. He lets Udayin finish, all of it, and when he answers, he starts by granting what's true in it. Third, the answer. In the poem, paraphrased here, the prince says: I don't despise the pleasures of the world. I know people are bound up in them. But I keep remembering that it all passes. Age is coming, and sickness, and death. If those three weren't real, I too would find delight here. Because they are, my heart can't settle into it. Not that pleasure is wicked: that it doesn't last, and he can't unsee it. Fourth, the tone. He answers without contempt, and even turns the advice around: if Udayin is truly his friend, why urge him toward what will end, instead of helping him find what won't? A disagreement between friends, with no one stomping off. And the king's plan fails again.

705.title: The plowed field
705.hook: he sees worms turned up by the plow and feels grief for them; then meets a wanderer (Buddhacarita 5)
705.howItsDone: Care for small creatures runs through Buddhist practice: the first precept is to refrain from taking life, and in some monastic traditions monks strain their drinking water or take care where they walk to avoid harming insects.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Udayin's advice, enjoy it while you're young, and the prince's kind reply. Your line: he answered gently.

Fresh soil, turned over in long rows. If you've ever dug a garden bed, you've seen what comes up with it: worms, grubs, beetles, small things suddenly in the open air, some of them cut in half by the blade. The prince, riding out toward the forest, stops his horse at the edge of a plowed field and looks. And the poem says what he feels. Not disgust. Not curiosity. Grief, the kind a person feels for family.
screen: `FRESH SOIL, TURNED OVER.` → `SMALL LIVES IN THE OPEN AIR.` → `HE STOPS AND LOOKS.`

segments.voice: First, the field. The ground has been torn by the plow, the young grass ripped up, and the earth is strewn with tiny creatures, insects and worms, killed or dying. The prince grieves, the poem says, as if his own kin had been slain. Second, the people. He sees the plowmen too, their bodies darkened by wind and sun and dust, and the oxen worn out from dragging the plow. The same mercy falls on all of them. Nobody in the field is the villain. Everyone in it is suffering something. Third, the stillness. He gets down from his horse, walks, sorrowful, and sits beneath a rose-apple tree. There he thinks about birth and death in the world, and his mind grows quiet and clear. The poem describes him settling into the first stage of deep meditation, right at the edge of a working field. And fourth, the visitor. A figure in a wanderer's robe comes toward him, someone the poem says no one else can see. He has left home, he says, afraid of birth and death, to seek freedom. Then, the poem says, he rises into the sky and is gone: a god in disguise, come to show the prince the road. So the poem joins the field and the fourth sight into one scene. First the grief, then the calm under the tree, and only then the wanderer, as if the prince had to feel for the smallest lives before he could see the way out for all of them.

706.title: The flight
706.hook: the palace asleep, the gates opening, the horse's hooves muffled (Buddhacarita 5)
706.howItsDone: The prince's leaving, often called the great going forth, is remembered in Buddhist art and at festivals, and in Theravada countries young men about to ordain sometimes ride in procession on a horse or are carried, recalling the prince's ride out of the city.

segments.voice: Yesterday: stillness under a rose-apple tree, after the prince grieved for small lives in a plowed field. Your line: grief for the small.

Before he leaves, he asks. That's the part of the flight that's easy to forget. The prince comes back from the field, goes to his father, bows, and says it out loud: let me go and become a wanderer. The king weeps. Not yet, he says. You're young. Wait. Then the prince makes an offer. Promise me four things, and I'll stay: that my life won't end in death, that sickness won't take my health, that age won't take my youth, that misfortune won't take what I have. The king can't promise any of them. Nobody could. And so the asking ends, and the night begins.

segments.voice: First, the sleeping palace. Back in his rooms the women play music for him as always, but the poem says the gods send a heavy sleep over them, and they fall where they are, instruments still in their arms. Year one stood in that room; tonight the poem only passes through it on the way to the door. Second, the horse. The prince wakes Chandaka, his attendant, and asks for Kanthaka, his horse. Chandaka brings him, and the prince speaks to the horse as to a friend, asking him to carry him well this one time. Third, the gates. All his life this palace has been a machine for keeping the prince in and the world out: heavy doors, bars, guards. Tonight, the poem says, gates that took strength to move swing open by themselves, without a sound. The city sleeps on. Fourth, the look back. Outside the city the prince turns toward it and vows not to come back until he has seen the far shore of birth and death. Then he rides on into the dark. A father built walls: a cleared road, a garden, a friend's advice, a palace full of music. One by one, they gave. Tonight, the last one does.

707.title: Chandaka sent back
707.hook: the charioteer begs to stay; the prince sends him home with his jewels (Buddhacarita 6)
707.howItsDone: The cutting of the hair and the change into a plain robe are remembered in Buddhist ordinations, where in some communities a new monk or nun has the head shaved and puts on the robe before taking vows.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the flight, the prince's night ride through gates that opened by themselves. Your line: the gates open.

Sunrise, and a horse that has run all night stands blowing at the edge of a hermitage. A young man climbs down. For the first time in his life, there is no palace behind him. Beside him stands Chandaka, the attendant who saddled the horse in the dark and rode out with him. He has done everything he was told all night. Now the prince gives him one more order: go home. And Chandaka says no.
screen: `SUNRISE AT THE HERMITAGE.` → `ONE MORE ORDER: GO HOME.` → `CHANDAKA SAYS NO.`

segments.voice: First, the thanks. Before any parting, the prince praises Chandaka: this loyalty, he says in paraphrase, is rare, a man who follows his master when there is nothing to gain by it. Second, the jewels. He takes off his ornaments and puts them in Chandaka's hands, with a message for the king. Tell my father I haven't gone into the forest out of anger, or for lack of love, or out of longing for heaven. I've gone to put an end to old age and death. Don't grieve for me. Third, the begging. Chandaka weeps. How can I lead this horse home with an empty saddle? What do I say to your father, to the queen who raised you, to your wife? The prince answers gently, with an image from the poem: beings meet the way birds gather in one tree for the night, and in the morning they fly off in different directions. Parting comes for everyone; this one, at least, has a purpose. Fourth, the last things. With his own sword the prince cuts off his long hair. A hunter in a dull-colored robe passes by, and the prince trades his fine silk clothes for that plain cloth; the poem says the hunter was a god in disguise. Then Chandaka turns for home, slowly, leading Kanthaka, and the poem says the horse licked the prince's feet and wept before he went. Since the old man on the cleared road, the poem has been taking things from the prince one at a time: his ease, a garden's charm, a friend's good argument, the palace. Today it's the jewels, his hair, his clothes and his last companion, and each one goes back with care.
screen: `FIRST, THE THANK-YOU.` · `THE JEWELS AND A MESSAGE.` · `BIRDS IN ONE TREE FOR A NIGHT.` · `HAIR CUT, SILK TRADED.` · then, large: `SENT HOME WITH THE JEWELS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you're holding that isn't really yours to keep: a borrowed book, a coat that hasn't left the closet in years, a job on a committee you agreed to long ago. Picture giving it back the way the prince did, thanks first, then a clear word about why, then open hands. Let your hands rest open in your lap for the rest of the sit.
Chandaka. The prince's attendant, thanked and sent home from the forest's edge with the horse, the jewels, and a message for the king. Today's word.
Your line: sent home with the jewels. Thanks first, then the honest reason. That's day seven hundred seven.

original.note: Sanskrit: the name of the prince's attendant; Pali tellings call him Channa.

trapdoor: what you thought: the prince just left his servant at the edge of the woods.
what it means: he thanks Chandaka, gives him the jewels and a message, and answers his tears before sending him home.
what a scholar hears: Ashvaghosha gives the servant a full speech of protest, so even this parting is argued out, like the leaving before it.

chat.says: What message did the prince send his father with the jewels?
options: That he left not in anger or for lack of love, but to end age and death.
That he was angry at being kept in the palace, and wouldn't forgive it.
That he'd come home in a year, once he had seen the wider world.
chat.meaning: Not anger, lack of love or longing for heaven: he tells Chandaka he has gone to put an end to old age and death.
